doc.title: Red Holloway interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995

title: Why he chose music: boxing, odd jobs, early pay, Eugene Wright
summary: Holloway explains that with few career options he turned to music, after boxing with Johnny Bratton; early pay was tiny but living was cheap.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Well, see I’ll be 68 years old this year. And when I was a kid, you could either be a Pullman porter, you could become a barber, if your folks had money you might be able to become a doctor. But if you had no talents and you were nice looking, you could become a pimp. But basically most people became, most men became Pullman porters. So I had none of those qualifications, and since my mother was a pianist and my father played violin, I decided maybe I should try to be a musician. But I always liked boxing because, you know like Sugar Ray and Joe Louis they were my idols, you know? And a friend of mine and I, we went to school together, named Johnny Bratton. We used to be in the gym together all the time, we used to run five miles a day for ten years. I started at about 8 or 9 years old, and he became — well we were amateur boxers. And he became a champion boxer, I don’t know if you’re familiar with Johnny Bratton, but he won one of those titles from Kid Gavilan from Cuba back in the 50s, but anyway, we were close friends. And I used to do this for a while, but I always liked music. But after about 37 amateur fights and getting my head smashed in, I really decided I should be a musician. And there were no, see in those days there were some real bad days back in the latter 30s and early 40s, and it was mean. So if you played music, there wasn’t a lot of money involved. They paid © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

like, well you made $2.50 an hour as a musician. And when you were making $6.00 a night and all you could eat and drink, that was good money. So basically that’s when I decided I really wanted to be a musician. And even though the money wasn’t an awful lot, you know, there wasn’t a requirement, the cost of living was down, so you didn’t have to pay a lot of money. You could rent a house for like $20 a month, stuff like that. And it was very cheap. Of course you didn’t make a lot of money but it didn’t cost a lot of money. In fact, my first job that I ever had – period -- was as a busboy for $9.98 — well actually it was $10.00, they took out two cents for Social Security — $9.98 a week, seven days a week, 7 ‘til 7. So I’m just saying this was back in the 40s, you know? So this is why I decided to be a musician, and so far I’ve managed to keep doing this. And I was raised in Chicago. I was born in Helena, Arkansas. But you know, in Chicago, this is where everybody from the south and everywhere, they would come to Chicago first and eventually they would move on to New York. And when I first really started making some what I call “serious money” I was working with Eugene Wright, I don’t know if you’re familiar with him, he was a bass player.
He played with Brubeck later, didn’t he?

Yeah. Senator Eugene Wright. I was in high school and he called me to work with his band. In fact I worked with his band until I went to the service. So like there were a lot of different reasons why I wanted to play music.
